summary: At the Passover table, Jesus gives the bread as His body and the cup as the new covenant in His blood, and commands, “do this in remembrance of Me.”
key_insight: Jesus took the meal that remembered Israel’s rescue from Egypt and gave it a new center. The bread Moses called “the bread of affliction” becomes “My body”; the cup becomes “My blood of the new covenant.” From that night, His people would remember a greater rescue, accomplished through His death.
story: As they were eating, Jesus took bread, blessed and broke it, and gave it to them, saying, “Take, eat; this is My body.” {Mk} It was given for them, and He told them, “do this in remembrance of Me.” {Lk}

Likewise He took the cup after supper. {Lk} He gave thanks and gave it to them, saying, “Drink from it, all of you. For this is My blood of the new covenant, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.” {Mt} And they all drank from it. {Mk} Luke gives His words this way: “This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is shed for you.” {Lk}
Then He said, “I will not drink of this fruit of the vine from now on until that day when I drink it new with you in My Father’s kingdom.” {Mt}
differences: Matthew and Mark say Jesus “blessed” the bread; Luke, like Paul (1 Corinthians 11:24), says He “gave thanks.”
Only Luke records “which is given for you; do this in remembrance of Me” over the bread, and says the cup came “after supper.”
Matthew and Mark read “This is My blood of the new covenant”; Luke reads “This cup is the new covenant in My blood.” Only Matthew adds “for the remission of sins.”
Matthew has Jesus say, “Drink from it, all of you”; Mark says, “they all drank from it.”
Matthew and Mark record the vow not to drink the fruit of the vine again after this cup; Luke records a similar vow earlier, with a cup before the bread (22:17–18).

fit.question: Matthew and Mark place Jesus’ vow not to drink “of the fruit of the vine” again after the cup of the Supper. Luke places a similar vow before the bread (Luke 22:17–18). When did Jesus say it?

points.label: Two cups, two sayings
points.text: Luke mentions two cups, one before the bread and one after supper (22:17, 20). Jesus may have spoken of not drinking again with the first cup and repeated it with the last, a natural repetition on a night of farewells.

points.label: Luke’s arrangement
points.text: Others think Luke placed the saying with the Passover cup to set the old feast and the new side by side, while Matthew and Mark kept it with the cup of the covenant.

fit.note: The words agree in substance; only their place in the meal differs, and both placements fit a long meal with more than one cup.
fit.short: Luke records two cups. Jesus likely spoke the vow with the first and repeated it with the last, or Luke arranged it by theme.

fit.question: Matthew and Mark record, “This is My blood of the new covenant.” Luke and Paul record, “This cup is the new covenant in My blood.” What exactly did Jesus say?

points.label: The same meaning
points.text: Both forms join the cup, His blood and the new covenant. Jesus probably spoke in Aramaic, and the Gospels give His words faithfully in Greek, without always giving them word for word.

points.label: Two early streams
points.text: Luke’s wording matches Paul’s, which Paul says he “received from the Lord” and passed on to the church (1 Corinthians 11:23). Matthew and Mark preserve another early form. Both were in use in the churches from the beginning.

fit.note: Small differences in wording show independent witnesses, not a changed message. Every account says the same thing about the cup.
fit.short: Both forms say the same thing: the cup is His blood, which makes the new covenant. The Gospels give the sense faithfully.

scene.label: Bread at the Passover
scene.text: At the Passover, the head of the household broke the unleavened bread, gave thanks, and explained what the meal meant, as Moses told fathers to answer their children’s questions (Exodus 12:26–27). Jesus did the familiar thing, then gave the bread a meaning no one at the table expected.

scene.label: Blood of the covenant
scene.text: At Mount Sinai, Moses sprinkled sacrificial blood on the people and said, “This is the blood of the covenant” (Exodus 24:8). Jeremiah later promised “a new covenant,” in which God would write His law on hearts and remember sins no more (Jeremiah 31:31–34). Jesus’ words join both promises.

scene.label: “For many”
scene.text: The phrase echoes Isaiah’s suffering Servant, who would “justify many” and “bore the sin of many” (Isaiah 53:11–12). Jesus is telling His disciples who He is and what His death will do.

scene.label: Remembrance
scene.text: In Scripture, to remember is more than to recall. Israel kept the Passover as “a memorial” so that each generation would share in the rescue (Exodus 12:14). Paul says that whenever believers eat this bread and drink this cup, they “proclaim the Lord’s death till He comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26).

scene.label: “This is My body”
scene.text: Churches understand Christ’s presence in the Supper differently. Some believe the bread and wine become, or truly bear, His body and blood; others, that Christ is present spiritually and received by faith; others see the meal chiefly as a memorial. All agree that Jesus gave it and that His people are to keep it.

witnesses.matthew: Adds the command “Drink from it, all of you” and the purpose of the blood: “for the remission of sins.” At Jesus’ birth Matthew explained His name: “He will save His people from their sins” (1:21). At this table Jesus shows how.
witnesses.mark: Gives the briefest account and notes simply that “they all drank from it.” Mark’s “shed for many” recalls Jesus’ earlier words that the Son of Man came “to give His life a ransom for many” (10:45).
witnesses.luke: Alone gives the command “do this in remembrance of Me” in the Gospels, stresses “for you,” and records two cups, setting the Supper inside the Passover meal. His wording closely matches Paul’s in 1 Corinthians 11, written about twenty-five years after the event, which shows how early the church was repeating these words.
witnesses.john: Does not record the bread and the cup. John tells of the same evening through the foot washing and Jesus’ long farewell (John 13–17).

seeing.reveals: Jesus explains His own death before it happens. His body is given and His blood poured out for others, to open a new covenant and bring forgiveness of sins. He is both the host who serves the meal and the sacrifice it remembers.
seeing.living: Come to the Lord’s Table as one for whom His body was given. It is not a routine, and it is not a prize for the worthy; it is His gift to sinners He has forgiven. Each time you eat and drink, you proclaim His death and wait for the day He drinks it new with you in His Father’s kingdom.
seeing.ponder: When you take the bread and the cup, do you receive them as His gift “for you”?

preaching.big_idea: At His table, Jesus explains His death: His body given and His blood shed for us.
outline: The cup: His blood of the new covenant (27–28)
The promise: a new cup in the kingdom (29)
preaching.watch_for: Jesus takes, blesses, breaks and gives, the same actions Matthew described at the feeding of the five thousand (14:19). The bread that once fed a crowd now pictures the body given for many.
